## Abstraction vs Encapsulation (Java)

Both are **OOP concepts**, but they solve **different problems**.

---

## 1. Abstraction

**Abstraction = hiding implementation details and showing only essential features.**

Used to focus on **what an object does**, not **how it works**.

Implemented using:

```text
Abstract classes
Interfaces
```

Example:

```java
interface Payment {

    void pay(double amount);

}

class CreditCardPayment implements Payment {

    public void pay(double amount) {
        System.out.println("Paid using credit card: " + amount);
    }

}
```

Usage:

```java
public class App {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Payment payment = new CreditCardPayment();

        payment.pay(500);

    }

}
```

User only sees:

```text
pay()
```

Implementation hidden.

---

## 2. Encapsulation

**Encapsulation = hiding internal data and controlling access using methods.**

Implemented using:

```text
private variables
getters/setters
```

Example:

```java
class User {

    private int age;

    public void setAge(int age) {

        if(age > 0) {
            this.age = age;
        }

    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }

}
```

Usage:

```java
User u = new User();

u.setAge(25);

System.out.println(u.getAge());
```

---

## Key Difference

| Feature | Abstraction | Encapsulation |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Hide implementation | Hide data |
| Focus | What object does | How data is protected |
| Implementation | Abstract class / Interface | Private fields + getters/setters |
| Level | Design level | Code level |

---

```text
Car

 stop()
 accelerate()
```

User doesn't know **engine mechanism**.

---

### Encapsulation

```text
Car
 private speed
 private fuel

 getSpeed()

```

Internal data protected.

## Proxy Pattern (Java)

The **Proxy Pattern** is a **structural design pattern** where a **proxy object acts as a substitute or intermediary for another object**.

The proxy **controls access to the real object**.

---

## Basic Idea

```text id="qhl0v0"
Client
   ↓
Proxy
   ↓
Real Object
```

The proxy can:

```text id="xcyq4d"
Add security
Add logging
Lazy loading
Control access
```

---

## Example Scenario

Example: **Image loading**

```text id="rxeh13"
Real image loading → expensive operation
Proxy image → loads only when needed
```

---

## Step 1 — Interface

```java id="7i1sd4"
interface Image {

    void display();

}
```

---

## Step 2 — Real Object

```java id="ddw5zt"
class RealImage implements Image {

    private String fileName;

    public RealImage(String fileName){

        this.fileName = fileName;
        loadFromDisk();

    }

    private void loadFromDisk(){
        System.out.println("Loading image: " + fileName);
    }

    public void display(){
        System.out.println("Displaying image: " + fileName);
    }

}
```

---

## Step 3 — Proxy Class

```java id="nyy70p"
class ProxyImage implements Image {

    private RealImage realImage;
    private String fileName;

    public ProxyImage(String fileName){
        this.fileName = fileName;
    }

    public void display(){

        if(realImage == null){
            realImage = new RealImage(fileName);
        }

        realImage.display();

    }

}
```

---

## Step 4 — Client Code

```java id="qzbhxj"
public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args){

        Image image = new ProxyImage("photo.jpg");

        image.display();   // loads and displays
        image.display();   // only displays

    }

}
```

Output

```text id="p1u6cb"
Loading image: photo.jpg
Displaying image: photo.jpg
Displaying image: photo.jpg
```

Image loads **only once**.

## HashMap vs ConcurrentHashMap (Java)

Both store **key–value pairs**, but they differ in **thread safety and concurrency handling**.

---

## 1. HashMap

`HashMap` is **not thread-safe**.

Example:

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Map<String,Integer> map = new HashMap<>();

        map.put("Java",1);
        map.put("Spring",2);

        System.out.println(map.get("Java"));

    }
}
```

Characteristics

```
Not synchronized
Not thread-safe
Allows 1 null key
Allows multiple null values
Faster in single-thread environments
```

Problem in multithreading:

```java
Map<String,Integer> map = new HashMap<>();

Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> map.put("A",1));
Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> map.put("B",2));

t1.start();
t2.start();
```

May cause **data inconsistency**.

---

## 2. ConcurrentHashMap

`ConcurrentHashMap` is **thread-safe and designed for high concurrency**.

Example:

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        ConcurrentHashMap<String,Integer> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

        map.put("Java",1);
        map.put("Spring",2);

        System.out.println(map.get("Java"));

    }
}
```

Characteristics

```
Thread-safe
Uses segment / bucket level locking
High concurrency
Better performance than synchronized collections
```

---

## Internal Working

### HashMap

```
Single structure
No locking
```

Multiple threads modifying it → **race condition**.

---

### ConcurrentHashMap

Java 7 concept:

```
Segment-level locking
```

Java 8 concept:

```
CAS (Compare-And-Swap)
Bucket-level locking
```

Example simplified idea:

```
Bucket 1 → lock
Bucket 2 → lock
Bucket 3 → lock
```

Multiple threads can operate **simultaneously on different buckets**.

---

## Null Handling

HashMap:

```java
Map<String,String> map = new HashMap<>();

map.put(null,"value");   // allowed
map.put("key",null);     // allowed
```

ConcurrentHashMap:

```java
ConcurrentHashMap<String,String> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

map.put(null,"value");   // NullPointerException
map.put("key",null);     // NullPointerException
```

---

## Key Differences

| Feature | HashMap | ConcurrentHashMap |
|---|---|---|
| Thread safety | No | Yes |
| Synchronization | None | Fine-grained locking |
| Null keys | Allowed | Not allowed |
| Null values | Allowed | Not allowed |
| Performance | Fast (single thread) | Fast in multi-thread |
| Use case | Single-thread apps | Concurrent systems |

---

## Example Real Use Case

```java
ConcurrentHashMap<String,Integer> counter = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

counter.compute("user", (k,v) -> v == null ? 1 : v + 1);
```

Thread-safe update.

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**HashMap is not thread-safe and allows null keys/values, while ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe, uses fine-grained locking for high concurrency, and does not allow null keys or values.**

## How `LinkedHashMap` Maintains Order (Java)

`LinkedHashMap` maintains **insertion order** using a **doubly linked list along with the hash table**.

So internally it uses:

```text
HashMap structure + Doubly Linked List
```

---

## Basic Example

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Map<Integer,String> map = new LinkedHashMap<>();

        map.put(3,"C");
        map.put(1,"A");
        map.put(2,"B");

        System.out.println(map);

    }
}
```

Output

```
{3=C, 1=A, 2=B}
```

Order is preserved.

---

## Internal Structure

`LinkedHashMap` extends `HashMap`.

Simplified node structure:

```java
static class Entry<K,V> extends HashMap.Node<K,V> {

    Entry<K,V> before;
    Entry<K,V> after;

}
```

Meaning:

```
prev pointer
next pointer
```

This creates a **doubly linked list of entries**.

---

## Data Structure View

Hash table for fast lookup:

```
Bucket Array
------------
0
1 → Node
2
3 → Node
```

Doubly linked list for order:

```
Head
 ↓
3=C ↔ 1=A ↔ 2=B
                 ↑
                Tail
```

Traversal uses the **linked list**, not bucket order.

---

## Insertion Flow

When inserting:

```java
map.put(5,"E");
```

Steps internally:

```
1 → calculate hash
2 → place node in bucket
3 → attach node to linked list tail
```

Pseudo idea:

```java
tail.after = newNode;
newNode.before = tail;
tail = newNode;
```

---

## Access Order Mode

`LinkedHashMap` can also maintain **access order**.

Example:

```java
LinkedHashMap<Integer,String> map =
        new LinkedHashMap<>(16,0.75f,true);
```

Third parameter:

```
true → access order
false → insertion order (default)
```

Example:

```java
map.put(1,"A");
map.put(2,"B");
map.put(3,"C");

map.get(1);
```

New order:

```
2=B → 3=C → 1=A
```

Recently accessed item moves to **end**.

---

## Used for LRU Cache

Example:

```java
class LRUCache<K,V> extends LinkedHashMap<K,V>{

    private int capacity;

    LRUCache(int capacity){
        super(capacity,0.75f,true);
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }

    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K,V> eldest){
        return size() > capacity;
    }
}
```

---

## Key Points

```
Uses HashMap for O(1) lookup
Uses doubly linked list for order
Maintains insertion order by default
Can maintain access order
```

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**LinkedHashMap maintains order by combining a hash table with a doubly linked list that keeps track of the insertion or access order of entries.**

## Java Agent

A **Java Agent** is a special Java program that can **modify or monitor the behavior of Java applications at runtime or during class loading**.

It is commonly used for:

```

Monitoring
Bytecode instrumentation

Security tools
```

## How Java Agent Works

A Java agent **intercepts class loading and modifies bytecode before the JVM executes it**.

Flow:

```
Application Start
        ↓
Java Agent
        ↓
ClassLoader loads class
        ↓
Agent modifies bytecode
        ↓
JVM executes modified class
```

## Difference Between `map()` and `flatMap()` (Java Streams)

Both are **intermediate operations in Stream API**, used to **transform data**, but they behave differently when the result is a **nested structure**.

---

# 1. `map()`

`map()` transforms **each element into another element**.

```text
1 input → 1 output
```

Example:

```java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        List<String> list = List.of("java","spring","react");

        List<String> result =
                list.stream()
                    .map(s -> s.toUpperCase())
                    .collect(Collectors.toList());

        System.out.println(result);

    }
}
```

Output

```
[JAVA, SPRING, REACT]
```

Transformation:

```
java   → JAVA
spring → SPRING
react  → REACT
```

---

# 2. `flatMap()`

`flatMap()` transforms each element into a **stream or collection**, then **flattens the result into a single stream**.

```text
1 input → multiple outputs
```

Example:

```java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        List<List<Integer>> list = List.of(
                List.of(1,2),
                List.of(3,4),
                List.of(5,6)
        );

        List<Integer> result =
                list.stream()
                    .flatMap(x -> x.stream())
                    .collect(Collectors.toList());

        System.out.println(result);

    }
}
```

Output

```
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
```

---

# Visual Difference

### Using `map()`

```
Input

[[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]]

map()

Output

Stream<Stream<Integer>>
```

---

### Using `flatMap()`

```
Input

[[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]]

flatMap()

Output

[1,2,3,4,5,6]
```

Flattened stream.

---

# Practical Example (Words)

```java
List<String> sentences =
        List.of("Java Spring", "React Node");
```

Using `map()`:

```java
sentences.stream()
         .map(s -> s.split(" "));
```

Result

```
Stream<String[]>
```

---

Using `flatMap()`:

```java
sentences.stream()
         .flatMap(s -> Arrays.stream(s.split(" ")))
         .forEach(System.out::println);
```

Output

```
Java
Spring
React
Node
```

---

# Key Differences

| Feature | map() | flatMap() |
|---|---|---|
| Transformation | One-to-one | One-to-many |
| Output | Stream of elements | Flattened stream |
| Nested streams | Possible | Removed |
| Common use | Simple transformations | Flatten nested collections |

---

**`map()` transforms each element into another element, while `flatMap()` transforms each element into a stream and flattens the result into a single stream.**

## Prefer Composition Over Inheritance (Java)

**Composition = a class contains another class as a field and uses its functionality.**

Instead of:

```text
IS-A relationship
```

composition uses:

```text
HAS-A relationship
```

---

## Example Using Inheritance (Not Always Good)

```java
class Engine {

    void start() {
        System.out.println("Engine started");
    }

}
```

Incorrect design with inheritance:

```java
class Car extends Engine {

}
```

Problem:

```text
Car IS-A Engine ❌
```

This relationship is **wrong**.

---

## Correct Design Using Composition

```java
class Engine {

    void start() {
        System.out.println("Engine started");
    }

}
```

Car has an engine:

```java
class Car {

    private Engine engine = new Engine();

    void startCar() {
        engine.start();
        System.out.println("Car started");
    }

}
```

Usage:

```java
public class App {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Car car = new Car();
        car.startCar();

    }

}
```

Output

```
Engine started
Car started
```

---

## Why Composition is Preferred

### 1. Avoids Tight Coupling

Inheritance creates strong dependency.

```text
Child tightly coupled to parent
```

Composition keeps classes **loosely coupled**.

---

### 2. Better Flexibility

You can change behavior easily.

```java
class ElectricEngine extends Engine { }
```

Use it:

```java
class Car {

    private Engine engine;

    Car(Engine engine){
        this.engine = engine;
    }

}
```

Usage:

```java
Car car = new Car(new ElectricEngine());
```

---

### 3. Prevents Wrong Relationships

Inheritance must represent:

```text
IS-A relationship
```

Example:

```
Dog IS-A Animal ✔
Car IS-A Engine ❌
```

Composition represents:

```text
HAS-A relationship
```

```
Car HAS-A Engine ✔
```

---

## Example Used in Real Systems

Java collections use composition.

```java
class HashSet<E> {

    private HashMap<E,Object> map;

}
```

Internally:

```text
HashSet HAS-A HashMap
```

---

## Key Differences

| Concept | Inheritance | Composition |
|---|---|---|
| Relationship | IS-A | HAS-A |
| Coupling | Tight | Loose |
| Flexibility | Less | More |
| Reusability | Limited | High |

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**Composition should be preferred over inheritance when classes share functionality but do not have a true IS-A relationship, allowing more flexible and loosely coupled designs using HAS-A relationships.**

Handling **distributed transactions** means maintaining **data consistency across multiple services or databases** in a distributed system.

Traditional ACID transactions do not work well across microservices, so different **patterns and tools** are used.

---

## 1. Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

Classic distributed transaction protocol.

Flow:

```text
Transaction Manager
      ↓
Prepare Phase
      ↓
Commit Phase
```

Steps:

```text
1 Coordinator asks all services to prepare
2 Services vote commit or rollback
3 If all commit → transaction commits
4 If any fails → rollback
```

Example architecture:

```text
Service A → DB1
Service B → DB2
Coordinator ensures both commit
```

Problem:

```text
Blocking
Slow
Poor scalability
```

Used in:

```text
JTA
XA Transactions
```

Example Java:

```java
UserTransaction tx = ctx.getUserTransaction();

tx.begin();

serviceA.save();
serviceB.save();

tx.commit();
```

---

## 2. Saga Pattern (Most Common)

Used in **microservices architecture**.

Instead of a global transaction, **each service performs a local transaction**.

If a step fails → **compensating transaction runs**.

Example flow:

```text
Order Service → Payment Service → Inventory Service
```

If payment fails:

```text
Compensate:
Cancel order
Release inventory
```

---

### Saga Choreography

Services communicate via **events**.

Example:

```text
OrderCreated → PaymentService
PaymentSuccess → InventoryService
InventoryReserved → OrderCompleted
```

Example with Kafka:

```java
kafkaTemplate.send("order-created", order);
```

Advantages:

```text
Highly scalable
Decoupled services
```

---

### Saga Orchestration

A **central orchestrator controls the workflow**.

Flow:

```text
Saga Orchestrator
      ↓
Order Service
      ↓
Payment Service
      ↓
Inventory Service
```

Example:

```java
orchestrator.executeSaga(orderId);
```

Tools:

```text
Camunda
Temporal
Netflix Conductor
```

---

## 3. Eventual Consistency

Instead of strict ACID:

```text
Data becomes consistent eventually
```

Example:

```text
Order placed → Payment processed → Inventory updated
```

Temporary inconsistency allowed.

Used in:

```text
High-scale systems
E-commerce
Social networks
```

---

## 4. Message Queue Based Transactions

Use message brokers to ensure reliability.

Example architecture:

```text
Service A → Kafka → Service B
```

Example:

```java
kafkaTemplate.send("payment-topic", paymentEvent);
```

Advantages:

```text
Reliable messaging
Retry mechanisms
Loose coupling
```

---

## 5. Idempotency

Ensure operations are **safe to retry**.

Example:

```java
if(paymentAlreadyProcessed(orderId)){
    return;
}
```

Prevents duplicate operations.

---

## Real Production Architecture

```text
Client
   ↓
Order Service
   ↓
Kafka Event
   ↓
Payment Service
   ↓
Inventory Service
```

Consistency achieved using:

```text
Saga pattern
Event-driven architecture
Retries + idempotency
```

## Fail-Fast vs Fail-Safe Iterator (Java)

Iterators define how collections behave when **modified during iteration**.

---

# 1. Fail-Fast Iterator

A **fail-fast iterator immediately throws `ConcurrentModificationException`** if the collection is structurally modified while iterating.

Used in most collections:

```text
ArrayList
HashMap
HashSet
TreeMap
```

---

## Example

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();

        list.add(1);
        list.add(2);
        list.add(3);

        for(Integer i : list) {

            list.add(4);   // modification during iteration

        }

    }

}
```

Result

```
ConcurrentModificationException
```

---

## Why This Happens

Collections maintain an internal counter:

```text
modCount
```

Iterator checks:

```text
expectedModCount == modCount
```

If mismatch → exception.

Simplified logic:

```java
if(modCount != expectedModCount)
    throw new ConcurrentModificationException();
```

---

# 2. Fail-Safe Iterator

A **fail-safe iterator works on a copy of the collection**, so modifications do not affect iteration.

Used in concurrent collections:

```text
ConcurrentHashMap
CopyOnWriteArrayList
CopyOnWriteArraySet
```

---

## Example

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        CopyOnWriteArrayList<Integer> list =
                new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

        list.add(1);
        list.add(2);
        list.add(3);

        for(Integer i : list) {

            list.add(4);   // allowed

        }

        System.out.println(list);

    }

}
```

Output

```
[1, 2, 3, 4]
```

No exception.

---

# Internal Concept

Fail-Fast

```
Original collection used
Modification detected
Exception thrown
```

Fail-Safe

```
Iterator works on snapshot copy
Original collection can change
No exception
```

---

# Key Differences

| Feature | Fail-Fast | Fail-Safe |
|---|---|---|
| Exception | Throws ConcurrentModificationException | No exception |
| Iteration source | Original collection | Copy of collection |
| Performance | Faster | More memory usage |
| Examples | ArrayList, HashMap | ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList |

---

# One-line Interview Answer

**Fail-fast iterators throw a `ConcurrentModificationException` if the collection is modified during iteration, while fail-safe iterators operate on a copy of the collection and allow modifications without throwing exceptions.**

## Parallel Stream (Java)

A **Parallel Stream** processes stream operations **using multiple threads simultaneously** to improve performance on large datasets.

It uses the **ForkJoinPool (common pool)** internally.

---

## Example

Sequential stream:

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        List<Integer> list = List.of(1,2,3,4,5);

        list.stream()
            .forEach(x -> System.out.println(
                    Thread.currentThread().getName() + " : " + x));

    }
}
```

Output (single thread):

```
main : 1
main : 2
main : 3
main : 4
main : 5
```

---

## Parallel Stream Example

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        List<Integer> list = List.of(1,2,3,4,5);

        list.parallelStream()
            .forEach(x -> System.out.println(
                    Thread.currentThread().getName() + " : " + x));

    }
}
```

Output example:

```
ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1 : 2
ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-3 : 5
ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-2 : 1
ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1 : 4
ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-3 : 3
```

Multiple threads execute tasks.

---

## Another Way to Create Parallel Stream

```java
list.stream()
    .parallel()
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

Equivalent to:

```java
list.parallelStream()
```

---

## Example Performance Scenario

```java
long sum =
        LongStream.rangeClosed(1,1_000_000_000)
                  .parallel()
                  .sum();

System.out.println(sum);
```

Parallel streams split the workload across CPU cores.

---

## Internal Working

Parallel stream uses **Fork/Join framework**.

Process:

```
Data Split
     ↓
Multiple Threads Process
     ↓
Results Combined
```

Example:

```
[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8]

Thread1 → [1,2]
Thread2 → [3,4]
Thread3 → [5,6]
Thread4 → [7,8]
```

---

## Important Points

```
Uses ForkJoinPool
Good for CPU-intensive tasks
Not always faster for small datasets
```

---

## Order Problem

Parallel streams may **not preserve order**.

Example:

```java
list.parallelStream()
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

Output may be random.

To maintain order:

```java
list.parallelStream()
    .forEachOrdered(System.out::println);
```

---

## When to Use Parallel Streams

Use when:

```
Large dataset
CPU intensive operations
Independent operations
```

Avoid when:

```
Small dataset
I/O operations
Shared mutable state
```

## Garbage Collection (GC) in Java

**Garbage Collection = automatic memory management** in the JVM that removes **objects from Heap memory which are no longer reachable**.

It helps prevent **memory leaks and manual memory deallocation**.

---

## Example

```java
public class GCExample {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        User u1 = new User();
        u1 = null;     // object becomes unreachable

    }

}

class User {
}
```

Flow:

```text
Heap
-----
User object  → unreachable
GC removes it
```

---

## How Garbage Collection Works (Step-by-Step)

### 1. Object Creation

Objects are created in **Heap memory (Eden space)**.

```java
User u = new User();
```

---

### 2. Reachability Check

GC checks whether objects are **reachable from GC Roots**.

GC Roots include:

```
Local variables in stack
Static variables
Active threads
JNI references
```

Example:

```java
User u = new User();
```

```text
Stack → reference → Heap object
```

Reachable → **not collected**

---

### 3. Unreachable Objects

If no reference points to object:

```java
User u = new User();
u = null;
```

Object becomes **eligible for garbage collection**.

---

## Heap Structure (Generational GC)

JVM divides heap into generations.

```
Heap
 ├── Young Generation
 │      ├── Eden
 │      ├── Survivor S0
 │      └── Survivor S1
 │
 └── Old Generation
```

---

### Young Generation

New objects are created here.

```
Eden → Survivor → Old
```

GC type:

```
Minor GC
```

---

### Old Generation

Objects that survive multiple GC cycles move here.

GC type:

```
Major GC / Full GC
```

---

## GC Algorithms

### 1. Mark and Sweep

```
Step 1 → Mark reachable objects
Step 2 → Remove unreachable objects
```

Example:

```
Heap
A → reachable
B → unreachable
C → reachable
```

GC removes **B**.

---

### 2. Mark and Compact

After deletion, memory is compacted.

```
Before

[A][ ][C][ ][ ]

After

[A][C][ ][ ][ ]
```

Reduces fragmentation.

---

### 3. Copying Algorithm

Used in **Young Generation**.

```
Eden → Survivor Space
```

Live objects copied, rest discarded.

---

## Popular Garbage Collectors

| GC | Use |
|---|---|
| Serial GC | Small apps |
| Parallel GC | High throughput |
| G1 GC | Default modern GC |
| ZGC | Low latency |
| Shenandoah | Low pause |

Example enabling G1:

```bash
java -XX:+UseG1GC App
```

---

```java

```

JVM **may ignore this request**.

```java
public class Demo {

        User u1 = new User();
        User u2 = new User();

    }
}
```

`u1` object → **eligible for GC**

```java

while(true){
    list.add(new byte[1024 * 1024]);
}
```

Heap fills → crash.

## Class Loading Mechanism (Java)

The **class loading mechanism** is the process by which the JVM **loads `.class` files into memory at runtime** and prepares them for execution.

The process is handled by **ClassLoaders**.

Flow:

```
Java Source (.java)
        ↓
Compilation
        ↓
Bytecode (.class)
        ↓
ClassLoader
        ↓
JVM Memory
```

---

# Phases of Class Loading

There are **3 main phases**.

```
Loading
Linking
Initialization
```

---

# 1. Loading

The JVM **loads the class bytecode into memory**.

Steps:

```
Locate .class file
Read bytecode
Create Class object
```

Example class:

```java
class User {

    static int count = 10;

}
```

JVM loads:

```
User.class → Method Area
```

---

# 2. Linking

Linking has **three steps**.

```
Verification
Preparation
Resolution
```

---

## Verification

JVM verifies bytecode correctness.

Checks:

```
Illegal code
Security violations
Invalid bytecode
```

Example issue detected:

```
Stack overflow in bytecode
Invalid memory access
```

---

## Preparation

Memory allocated for **static variables**.

Example:

```java
class Test {

    static int x = 10;

}
```

Preparation step:

```
x = 0   // default value
```

---

## Resolution

Symbolic references are replaced with **direct references**.

Example:

```
Method calls
Field references
Interface references
```

---

# 3. Initialization

Static variables are assigned **actual values** and static blocks execute.

Example:

```java
class Test {

    static int x = 10;

    static {
        System.out.println("Class initialized");
    }

}
```

Initialization result:

```
x = 10
Static block executed
```

---

# Complete Flow

```
Loading
   ↓
Verification
   ↓
Preparation
   ↓
Resolution
   ↓
Initialization
```

---

# Example Showing Class Loading

```java
class Demo {

    static {
        System.out.println("Class Loaded");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        System.out.println("Main method");

    }
}
```

Output

```
Class Loaded
Main method
```

---

# Key Points

```
Classes are loaded only when needed
Handled by ClassLoaders
Loaded into Method Area
Ensures security and correctness
```

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**The class loading mechanism is the process by which the JVM dynamically loads `.class` files into memory, verifies them, prepares memory for variables, resolves references, and initializes the class before execution.**

Handling **concurrency in microservices** means ensuring **multiple requests or services modifying the same data do not cause inconsistency, race conditions, or data corruption**.

In production systems, this is solved using **database techniques, distributed locks, messaging patterns, and idempotency**.

---

## 1. Optimistic Locking (Most Common)

Uses a **version field** to detect concurrent updates.

### Example (JPA)

```java
@Entity
class Order {

    @Id
    private Long id;

    @Version
    private Long version;

    private String status;

}
```

Update flow:

```text
Thread1 reads version = 1
Thread2 reads version = 1

Thread1 updates → version = 2
Thread2 update fails → OptimisticLockException
```

Retry logic:

```java
try {
    orderRepository.save(order);
} catch (OptimisticLockException e) {
    retry();
}
```

Best for:

```text
Low conflict scenarios
High throughput systems
```

---

## 2. Pessimistic Locking

Database-level locking prevents other transactions from updating the row.

### Example

```java
@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
@Query("SELECT o FROM Order o WHERE o.id = :id")
Order findOrderForUpdate(Long id);
```

Flow:

```text
Thread1 locks row
Thread2 waits
```

Best for:

```text
High-conflict operations
Financial transactions
```

---

## 3. Distributed Lock (Redis / ZooKeeper)

Used when multiple service instances modify shared resources.

Example using Redis:

```java
RLock lock = redissonClient.getLock("order-lock");

lock.lock();

try {
    processOrder();
} finally {
    lock.unlock();
}
```

Popular tools:

```text
Redis (Redisson)
ZooKeeper
Etcd
```

---

## 4. Idempotency

Ensure repeated requests do not cause duplicate operations.

Example:

```java
if(paymentRepository.existsByTransactionId(txId)){
    return;
}
```

Used for:

```text
Payments
Order processing
Retry handling
```

---

## 5. Event-Driven Architecture

Use messaging to process events sequentially.

Example:

```text
Order Service → Kafka → Payment Service
```

Kafka guarantees ordering per partition.

Example consumer:

```java
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders")
public void process(OrderEvent event){
    handleOrder(event);
}
```

Benefits:

```text
Async processing
Decoupled services
Better scalability
```

---

## 6. Saga Pattern

Used when multiple services update data.

Example:

```text
Order Service → Payment Service → Inventory Service
```

If failure occurs:

```text
Compensation transaction executed
```

Ensures consistency across services.

---

## 7. Rate Limiting

Prevent overload and concurrent spikes.

Example using Bucket4j:

```java
Bucket bucket = Bucket4j.builder()
        .addLimit(Bandwidth.simple(100, Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
        .build();
```

---

```text
   ↓

   ↓
Load Balancer
   ↓

   ↓
Redis Lock / Optimistic Lock
   ↓

   ↓

```


## Metaspace (Java)

**Metaspace is a memory area in the JVM used to store class metadata.**

It was introduced in **Java 8** to replace **PermGen (Permanent Generation)**.

Location:

```text
Native Memory (outside heap)
```

---

## What Metaspace Stores

Metaspace stores **class-level metadata**, such as:

```
Class structure
Method metadata
Static fields
Constant pool
ClassLoader information
```

Example:

```java
class User {

    static int count = 10;

    void display(){
        System.out.println("User class");
    }

}
```

Stored in Metaspace:

```
Class metadata
Method info
Static variables
```

---

## JVM Memory Layout (Java 8+)

```
JVM Memory

Heap
 ├─ Young Generation
 └─ Old Generation

Metaspace
 └─ Class Metadata
```

Metaspace is **separate from heap memory**.

---

## Before Java 8 (PermGen)

Older JVM versions used **PermGen**.

```
Heap
 ├─ Young
 ├─ Old
 └─ PermGen
```

Problem:

```
Fixed size
Frequent OutOfMemoryError
```

Example error:

```
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space
```

---

## Why Metaspace Was Introduced

Metaspace solves PermGen limitations.

Advantages:

```
Uses native memory
Dynamic resizing
Better class loading performance
Reduced memory errors
```

---

## Metaspace Configuration

Set maximum size:

```bash
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m
```

Initial size:

```bash
-XX:MetaspaceSize=128m
```

---

## Metaspace OutOfMemory Example

Occurs when too many classes are loaded.

Example:

```java
while(true){
    new CustomClassLoader().loadClass("User");
}
```

Error:

```
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace
```

---

## Key Differences: PermGen vs Metaspace

| Feature | PermGen | Metaspace |
|---|---|---|
| Java version | ≤ Java 7 | Java 8+ |
| Memory location | Heap | Native memory |
| Size | Fixed | Dynamic |
| Error | PermGen space | Metaspace |

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**Metaspace is a JVM memory area introduced in Java 8 that stores class metadata in native memory, replacing the older PermGen space.**

## TreeMap vs HashMap (Java)

Both store **key–value pairs**, but they differ in **ordering, performance, and internal structure**.

---

## 1. HashMap

`HashMap` stores entries using **hashing and bucket arrays**.

Example:

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Map<Integer,String> map = new HashMap<>();

        map.put(3,"C");
        map.put(1,"A");
        map.put(2,"B");

        System.out.println(map);

    }
}
```

Possible output:

```
{3=C, 1=A, 2=B}
```

Characteristics

```
No ordering
Fast access
Uses hash table
```

---

## 2. TreeMap

`TreeMap` stores entries using a **Red-Black Tree**.

Example:

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Map<Integer,String> map = new TreeMap<>();

        map.put(3,"C");
        map.put(1,"A");
        map.put(2,"B");

        System.out.println(map);

    }
}
```

Output (sorted):

```
{1=A, 2=B, 3=C}
```

Characteristics

```
Sorted by keys
Uses Red-Black Tree
Maintains natural ordering
```

---

## Internal Structure

### HashMap

```
Array → Bucket → LinkedList / Tree
```

Example:

```
Bucket[3] → (3,C)
Bucket[1] → (1,A)
```

---

### TreeMap

```
        2
       / \
      1   3
```

Balanced **Red-Black Tree**.

---

## Time Complexity

| Operation | HashMap | TreeMap |
|---|---|---|
| put() | O(1) avg | O(log n) |
| get() | O(1) avg | O(log n) |
| remove() | O(1) avg | O(log n) |

---

## Null Handling

HashMap:

```java
Map<String,String> map = new HashMap<>();

map.put(null,"value"); // allowed
```

TreeMap:

```java
Map<String,String> map = new TreeMap<>();

map.put(null,"value"); // NullPointerException
```

---

## Sorting Example (TreeMap)

```java
TreeMap<Integer,String> map = new TreeMap<>();

map.put(5,"E");
map.put(1,"A");
map.put(3,"C");

System.out.println(map.firstKey());
System.out.println(map.lastKey());
```

Output

```
1
5
```

---

## Key Differences

| Feature | HashMap | TreeMap |
|---|---|---|
| Ordering | No ordering | Sorted by key |
| Data structure | Hash table | Red-Black Tree |
| Performance | Faster | Slower |
| Null key | Allowed (1) | Not allowed |
| Use case | Fast lookup | Sorted data |

---

## When to Use

Use **HashMap** when:

```
Fast access needed
Ordering not required
```

Use **TreeMap** when:

```
Sorted keys needed
Range queries required
```

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**HashMap stores key–value pairs using hashing and provides fast O(1) access without ordering, while TreeMap stores entries in a sorted order using a Red-Black Tree with O(log n) operations.**

## HashMap vs HashTable (Java)

Both store **key–value pairs**, but they differ in **thread safety, performance, and design**.

---

## 1. HashMap

`HashMap` is **not synchronized** and is faster.

Example:

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Map<String,Integer> map = new HashMap<>();

        map.put("Java",1);
        map.put("Spring",2);

        System.out.println(map.get("Java"));

    }
}
```

Features:

```text
Not thread-safe
Allows one null key
Allows multiple null values
Faster
```

Example with null:

```java
Map<String,String> map = new HashMap<>();

map.put(null,"value");
map.put("key",null);
```

---

## 2. HashTable

`HashTable` is **synchronized** and thread-safe.

Example:

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Hashtable<String,Integer> table = new Hashtable<>();

        table.put("Java",1);
        table.put("Spring",2);

        System.out.println(table.get("Java"));

    }
}
```

Features:

```text
Thread-safe
Does not allow null key
Does not allow null value
Slower due to synchronization
```

Invalid:

```java
Hashtable<String,String> table = new Hashtable<>();

table.put(null,"value");  // NullPointerException
```

---

## Internal Structure

Both use **hashing and buckets**.

```text
Key → hashCode() → bucket index → value
```

Example concept:

```text
Bucket Array
------------
0
1 → (key,value)
2
3 → (key,value)
```

---

## Thread Safety Example

HashMap (not safe):

```java
Map<String,Integer> map = new HashMap<>();
```

Better modern alternative:

```java
Map<String,Integer> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
```

---

## Key Differences

| Feature | HashMap | HashTable |
|---|---|---|
| Synchronization | Not synchronized | Synchronized |
| Thread safety | Not thread-safe | Thread-safe |
| Null key | Allowed (1) | Not allowed |
| Null value | Allowed | Not allowed |
| Performance | Faster | Slower |
| Introduced | Java 1.2 | Java 1.0 |

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**HashMap is a non-synchronized, faster collection that allows one null key and multiple null values, while HashTable is synchronized, thread-safe, and does not allow null keys or values.**

## What Happens When HashMap Collisions Occur

A **collision** occurs when **two different keys produce the same bucket index**.

Meaning:

```text
key1.hashCode() % capacity = same index
key2.hashCode() % capacity = same index
```

Both keys go into the **same bucket**.

---

## Example

```java
Map<Integer,String> map = new HashMap<>();

map.put(10,"A");
map.put(26,"B");
```

Assume capacity:

```
capacity = 16
```

Hash calculation:

```
10 % 16 = 10
26 % 16 = 10
```

Both go to **bucket 10** → collision.

---

## Step 1 — Linked List Creation

When collision happens, `HashMap` stores entries as a **linked list**.

Structure:

```
Bucket[10]

[10,A] → [26,B]
```

Internal node structure:

```java
static class Node<K,V> {
    int hash;
    K key;
    V value;
    Node<K,V> next;
}
```

---

## Step 2 — Searching During `get()`

Example:

```java
map.get(26);
```

Steps:

```
1 → calculate hash
2 → find bucket index
3 → traverse nodes
4 → compare using equals()
```

Pseudo logic:

```java
if(node.hash == hash && node.key.equals(key)){
    return node.value;
}
```

---

## Step 3 — Treeification (Java 8)

If bucket size exceeds **8 elements**, linked list converts into a **Red-Black Tree**.

```
LinkedList → RedBlackTree
```

Why?

```
LinkedList search → O(n)
Tree search → O(log n)
```

Example bucket:

```
Before

A → B → C → D → E → F → G → H → I
```

After treeify:

```
        D
      /   \
     B     G
    / \   / \
   A   C F   I
```

---

## Step 4 — Untreeify

If entries fall below **6 nodes**, tree converts back to **linked list**.

```
Tree → LinkedList
```

---

## Important Thresholds (Java 8)

```
TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8
UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6
MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64
```

Meaning:

```
Tree conversion only if table size ≥ 64
```

---

## Time Complexity

| Case | Complexity |
|-----|-----|
| Normal | O(1) |
| Collision (list) | O(n) |
| Collision (tree) | O(log n) |

---

## Example

```java
Map<Integer,String> map = new HashMap<>();

map.put(1,"A");
map.put(17,"B");
map.put(33,"C");

System.out.println(map.get(33));
```

Even with collisions → HashMap finds correct value.

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**When collisions occur in a HashMap, multiple entries are stored in the same bucket using a linked list, and in Java 8+, if the list exceeds a threshold (8), it is converted into a red-black tree to improve lookup performance.**

## CompletableFuture (Java)

`CompletableFuture` is a **class in `java.util.concurrent` used for asynchronous programming**.  
It allows you to **run tasks in the background and process results later without blocking the main thread**.

Introduced in **Java 8**.

Package:

```java
java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture
```

---

# Basic Example

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        CompletableFuture<String> future =
                CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Hello Java");

        System.out.println(future.get());

    }
}
```

Output

```
Hello Java
```

Task runs **asynchronously in another thread**.

---

# Running Async Task (No Return)

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        CompletableFuture.runAsync(() ->
                System.out.println("Async task running"));

    }
}
```

Methods used:

```
runAsync() → no result
supplyAsync() → returns result
```

---

# Processing Result

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 10)
                .thenApply(x -> x * 2)
                .thenAccept(System.out::println);

    }
}
```

Output

```
20
```

Flow:

```
10 → thenApply → multiply → thenAccept → print
```

---

# Chaining Multiple Async Tasks

```java
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Java")
        .thenApply(s -> s + " Stream")
        .thenApply(String::toUpperCase)
        .thenAccept(System.out::println);
```

Output

```
JAVA STREAM
```

---

# Combining Two Futures

```java
CompletableFuture<Integer> f1 =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 10);

CompletableFuture<Integer> f2 =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 20);

CompletableFuture<Integer> result =
        f1.thenCombine(f2, (a,b) -> a + b);

System.out.println(result.join());
```

Output

```
30
```

---

# Handling Exceptions

```java
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 10/0)
        .exceptionally(ex -> {
            System.out.println("Error: " + ex);
            return 0;
        })
        .thenAccept(System.out::println);
```

Output

```
Error: java.lang.ArithmeticException
0
```

---

# Running Multiple Futures

```java
CompletableFuture<Void> all =
        CompletableFuture.allOf(f1, f2);

all.join();
```

Waits for **all tasks to complete**.

---

# Important Methods

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `runAsync()` | Async task without result |
| `supplyAsync()` | Async task with result |
| `thenApply()` | Transform result |
| `thenAccept()` | Consume result |
| `thenCombine()` | Combine two futures |
| `exceptionally()` | Handle errors |
| `allOf()` | Wait for multiple tasks |

---

# Why CompletableFuture is Powerful

```
Non-blocking programming
Async pipelines
Task composition
Parallel execution
Better than Future API
```

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**CompletableFuture is a Java class used for asynchronous programming that allows running tasks in the background and chaining or combining results without blocking the main thread.**

## Difference Between `forEach()` and `forEachOrdered()` (Java Streams)

Both are **terminal operations** used to iterate through elements of a stream.

They mainly differ in **order handling during parallel streams**.

---

# 1. `forEach()`

`forEach()` processes elements **without guaranteeing order**, especially in **parallel streams**.

Example:

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        List<Integer> list = List.of(1,2,3,4,5);

        list.parallelStream()
            .forEach(System.out::println);

    }
}
```

Possible output:

```
3
1
5
2
4
```

Reason:

```
Multiple threads process elements simultaneously
Order is not guaranteed
```

---

# 2. `forEachOrdered()`

`forEachOrdered()` **preserves the encounter order** of the stream.

Example:

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        List<Integer> list = List.of(1,2,3,4,5);

        list.parallelStream()
            .forEachOrdered(System.out::println);

    }
}
```

Output:

```
1
2
3
4
5
```

Even with parallel processing, order is maintained.

---

# Sequential Stream Case

With normal stream:

```java
list.stream().forEach(System.out::println);
```

Both behave the same because execution is **single-threaded**.

---

# Key Differences

| Feature | forEach() | forEachOrdered() |
|---|---|---|
| Order guarantee | No | Yes |
| Parallel stream behavior | Unordered | Maintains order |
| Performance | Faster | Slightly slower |
| Use case | When order not required | When order matters |

---

# Example Showing Difference

```java
List<Integer> list = List.of(1,2,3,4,5);

System.out.println("forEach:");

list.parallelStream()
    .forEach(System.out::print);

System.out.println("\nforEachOrdered:");

list.parallelStream()
    .forEachOrdered(System.out::print);
```

Possible output:

```
forEach:
35214

forEachOrdered:
12345
```

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**`forEach()` processes elements without guaranteeing order in parallel streams, while `forEachOrdered()` preserves the encounter order even when the stream is processed in parallel.**

## How `HashMap` Works Internally (Java)

`HashMap` stores **key–value pairs** using a **hashing mechanism and bucket array**.

Basic structure:

```
Key → hashCode() → bucket index → store value
```

---

## 1. HashMap Structure

Internally it uses an **array of buckets**.

```java
Node<K,V>[] table;
```

Each bucket contains **Node objects**.

Simplified node structure:

```java
static class Node<K,V> {

    final int hash;
    final K key;
    V value;
    Node<K,V> next;

}
```

Meaning:

```
hash
key
value
next (for collision chain)
```

---

## 2. Putting Data (`put()`)

Example:

```java
Map<String,Integer> map = new HashMap<>();

map.put("Java",1);
map.put("Spring",2);
```

Internal steps:

```
1 → calculate hashCode()
2 → convert hash → index
3 → store in bucket
```

Simplified code logic:

```java
int hash = key.hashCode();

int index = hash % table.length;

table[index] = new Node(hash,key,value);
```

---

## 3. Hash Calculation (Java 8)

```java
static final int hash(Object key) {
    int h;
    return (key == null) ? 0 : (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16);
}
```

Purpose:

```
Better hash distribution
Reduce collisions
```

---

## 4. Bucket Index

Index calculation:

```java
index = (n - 1) & hash
```

Example:

```
table size = 16
hash = 21

index = (16-1) & 21
index = 5
```

So element stored in **bucket 5**.

---

## 5. Collision Handling

Collision occurs when **two keys map to same bucket**.

Example:

```
Key1 → index 5
Key2 → index 5
```

Structure becomes:

```
Bucket[5]

Key1 → Value1
   ↓
Key2 → Value2
```

Linked list chain.

---

## 6. Tree Conversion (Java 8)

If bucket size exceeds **8 nodes**, list becomes **Red-Black Tree**.

```
LinkedList → Red Black Tree
```

Why?

```
Improve search time
```

Time complexity:

```
LinkedList → O(n)
Tree → O(log n)
```

---

## 7. Retrieving Data (`get()`)

Example:

```java
map.get("Java");
```

Steps:

```
1 → calculate hashCode
2 → find bucket index
3 → traverse nodes
4 → match key using equals()
```

Simplified logic:

```java
if(node.hash == hash && node.key.equals(key)){
    return node.value;
}
```

---

## 8. Resizing (Rehashing)

Default capacity:

```
16
```

Default load factor:

```
0.75
```

Resize condition:

```
size > capacity × loadFactor
```

Example:

```
16 × 0.75 = 12
```

After 12 elements → resize to **32**.

---

## 9. Time Complexity

| Operation | Complexity |
|---|---|
| put() | O(1) average |
| get() | O(1) average |
| collision list | O(n) |
| tree bucket | O(log n) |

---

## Example Demonstration

```java
Map<Integer,String> map = new HashMap<>();

map.put(1,"A");
map.put(2,"B");
map.put(3,"C");

System.out.println(map.get(2));
```

Output

```
B
```

---

## Important Interview Points

```
Uses array + linked list + red-black tree
HashCode determines bucket
equals() confirms key match
Load factor controls resize
Treeification occurs after 8 nodes
```

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**HashMap internally uses an array of buckets where each bucket stores nodes using hashing; collisions are handled using linked lists and converted to red-black trees in Java 8 to maintain efficient lookup performance.**

## Thread Pool (Java)

A **Thread Pool** is a group of **pre-created reusable threads** used to execute multiple tasks efficiently.

Instead of creating a new thread for every task, tasks are **submitted to the pool and executed by available threads**.

Java provides thread pools via:

```java
java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService
```

---

## Example Without Thread Pool

Creating new thread for each task:

```java
public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        for(int i=0;i<5;i++){

            Thread t = new Thread(() ->
                    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()));

            t.start();
        }

    }
}
```

Problem:

```
Too many threads created
High memory usage
Context switching overhead
```

---

## Example Using Thread Pool

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        ExecutorService executor =
                Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3);

        for(int i=0;i<6;i++){

            executor.submit(() ->
                    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()));
        }

        executor.shutdown();
    }
}
```

Output example:

```
pool-1-thread-1
pool-1-thread-2
pool-1-thread-3
pool-1-thread-1
pool-1-thread-2
pool-1-thread-3
```

Threads are **reused**.

---

## How Thread Pool Works

```
Tasks submitted
      ↓
Task Queue
      ↓
Available Thread picks task
      ↓
Task executed
      ↓
Thread returns to pool
```

---

## Types of Thread Pools

### Fixed Thread Pool

```java
ExecutorService executor =
        Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5);
```

Fixed number of threads.

---

### Cached Thread Pool

```java
ExecutorService executor =
        Executors.newCachedThreadPool();
```

Creates threads as needed.

---

### Single Thread Pool

```java
ExecutorService executor =
        Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
```

Single worker thread.

---

### Scheduled Thread Pool

```java
ScheduledExecutorService executor =
        Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2);
```

Runs scheduled tasks.

---

## Example with Callable

```java
ExecutorService executor =
        Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);

Future<Integer> result =
        executor.submit(() -> 10 + 20);

System.out.println(result.get());

executor.shutdown();
```

Output

```
30
```

---

## Benefits

```
Better performance
Thread reuse
Reduced overhead
Controlled concurrency
```

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**A Thread Pool is a collection of reusable worker threads that execute submitted tasks, improving performance by reducing the overhead of creating and destroying threads.**

## Class Loaders (Java)

**ClassLoaders are components of the JVM responsible for loading `.class` files into memory at runtime.**

They convert **bytecode (.class files) → Class objects inside JVM**.

Basic flow:

```
.class file
     ↓
ClassLoader
     ↓
Class Object in JVM
```

Example:

```java
public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        System.out.println("Class loaded by: " +
                Demo.class.getClassLoader());

    }
}
```

---

# Types of ClassLoaders

Java has **three main class loaders**.

```
Bootstrap ClassLoader
        ↓
Extension ClassLoader
        ↓
Application ClassLoader
```

---

# 1. Bootstrap ClassLoader

The **root class loader**.

Loads **core Java classes**.

Examples:

```
java.lang.String
java.lang.Object
java.util.*
```

Location:

```
<JAVA_HOME>/lib
```

Example:

```java
System.out.println(String.class.getClassLoader());
```

Output

```
null
```

(`null` means bootstrap loader in JVM)

---

# 2. Extension ClassLoader

Loads classes from **Java extension libraries**.

Location:

```
<JAVA_HOME>/lib/ext
```

Example:

```java
System.out.println(
        javax.crypto.Cipher.class.getClassLoader());
```

---

# 3. Application ClassLoader

Loads classes from the **application classpath**.

Examples:

```
Your project classes
External libraries
Spring Boot classes
```

Example:

```java
System.out.println(Demo.class.getClassLoader());
```

Output example:

```
jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader
```

---

# ClassLoader Delegation Model

Class loaders follow **parent delegation model**.

Process:

```
Application ClassLoader
        ↓
Extension ClassLoader
        ↓
Bootstrap ClassLoader
```

Steps:

```
1 Check if class already loaded
2 Delegate request to parent
3 Parent tries to load class
4 If parent fails → child loads class
```

---

# Example Flow

Loading `java.lang.String`:

```
Application Loader → asks parent
Extension Loader → asks parent
Bootstrap Loader → loads String class
```

---

# Custom ClassLoader Example

```java
class MyClassLoader extends ClassLoader {

    @Override
    protected Class<?> findClass(String name)
            throws ClassNotFoundException {

        byte[] data = loadClassData(name);

        return defineClass(name, data, 0, data.length);
    }

    private byte[] loadClassData(String name){
        return new byte[0];
    }
}
```

Used in:

```
Application servers
Plugin systems
Dynamic class loading
```

---

# Key Points

```
Responsible for loading classes into JVM
Follow parent delegation model
Improve security
Avoid duplicate class loading
```

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**ClassLoaders are JVM components responsible for dynamically loading `.class` files into memory, following a parent delegation model with Bootstrap, Extension, and Application class loaders.**

## Set vs List (Java)

Both are part of the **Java Collections Framework**, but they differ in **ordering, duplicates, and indexing**.

---

## 1. List

`List` is an **ordered collection** that allows **duplicates**.

Common implementations:

```text
ArrayList
LinkedList
Vector
```

Example:

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();

        list.add("Java");
        list.add("Spring");
        list.add("Java");

        System.out.println(list);

    }

}
```

Output

```
[Java, Spring, Java]
```

Features:

```
Maintains insertion order
Allows duplicates
Supports index access
```

Example using index:

```java
System.out.println(list.get(1));
```

---

## 2. Set

`Set` is a **collection that does not allow duplicate elements**.

Common implementations:

```text
HashSet
LinkedHashSet
TreeSet
```

Example:

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Set<String> set = new HashSet<>();

        set.add("Java");
        set.add("Spring");
        set.add("Java");

        System.out.println(set);

    }

}
```

Output

```
[Java, Spring]
```

Duplicate `"Java"` removed.

---

## Ordering Behavior

HashSet:

```
No guaranteed order
```

LinkedHashSet:

```
Maintains insertion order
```

TreeSet:

```
Sorted order
```

Example:

```java
Set<Integer> set = new TreeSet<>();

set.add(5);
set.add(1);
set.add(3);

System.out.println(set);
```

Output

```
[1, 3, 5]
```

---

## Key Differences

| Feature | List | Set |
|---|---|---|
| Duplicates | Allowed | Not allowed |
| Order | Maintains insertion order | Usually unordered |
| Index access | Supported | Not supported |
| Common implementations | ArrayList, LinkedList | HashSet, TreeSet |

---

## Example Comparison

```java
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(1);
list.add(1);

Set<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();
set.add(1);
set.add(1);

System.out.println(list.size()); // 2
System.out.println(set.size());  // 1
```

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**List is an ordered collection that allows duplicate elements and supports index-based access, while Set is a collection that does not allow duplicate elements and typically does not provide index-based access.**

## Bytecode (Java)

**Bytecode is the intermediate code generated by the Java compiler (`javac`) from Java source code.**

It is stored in:

```text
.class file
```

Bytecode is **platform-independent**, which enables Java’s **Write Once Run Anywhere (WORA)** principle.

---

## Compilation Flow

```text
Java Source Code (.java)
        ↓
javac compiler
        ↓
Bytecode (.class)
        ↓
JVM
        ↓
Machine Code
```

## Example

Java source code:

```java
public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        int a = 10;
        int b = 20;
```

## Why Bytecode is Important

Bytecode provides:

```
Portability
```

Since JVM interprets bytecode, the same `.class` file can run on:

```
Windows
Linux
Mac
```

As long as JVM is installed.

## JVM Execution of Bytecode

JVM executes bytecode using:

```
Interpreter
```

Flow:

```
   ↓
```

```
Call object method
```

**Bytecode is the platform-independent intermediate code generated by the Java compiler from `.java` files, which is executed by the JVM.**
What is Collectors API?

Tracing requests in microservices is done using **distributed tracing**, which allows you to **track a single request as it travels across multiple services**.

This helps debug **latency issues, failures, and service dependencies**.

---

**1. Use Trace IDs and Span IDs**

Each request gets a **Trace ID** and every service call generates a **Span ID**.

Flow:

```text id="3mzkjq"
Client Request
   ↓
Trace ID generated
   ↓
Service A (Span1)
   ↓
Service B (Span2)
   ↓
```

## What Happens If an Exception Is Not Handled (Java)

If an **exception is not handled using `try-catch`**, the JVM **propagates it up the call stack**.

If no method handles it, the **JVM terminates the program and prints a stack trace**.

---

## Example

```java
public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        int a = 10;
        int b = 0;

        int result = a / b;

        System.out.println(result);

    }
}
```

Output:

```text
Exception in thread "main"
java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero
    at Demo.main(Demo.java:7)
```

Program **stops immediately**.

---

## Exception Propagation

Example:

```java
public class Demo {

    static void method3() {
        int x = 10 / 0;
    }

    static void method2() {
        method3();
    }

    static void method1() {
        method2();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        method1();
    }

}
```

Flow:

```text
method3()
   ↓
method2()
   ↓
method1()
   ↓
main()
   ↓
JVM handles exception
```

If none handle it → **program terminates**.

---

## Stack Trace Meaning

Example output:

```text
Exception in thread "main"
java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero
    at Demo.method3(Demo.java:5)
    at Demo.method2(Demo.java:9)
    at Demo.method1(Demo.java:13)
    at Demo.main(Demo.java:17)
```

Explanation:

```text
Shows method call chain
Helps debugging
```

---

## Checked Exception Case

Checked exceptions **must be handled or declared**.

Example:

```java
import java.io.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        FileReader file = new FileReader("test.txt");

    }

}
```

Compile error:

```text
Unhandled exception type FileNotFoundException
```

---

## Key Points

```text
Unchecked exception → program crashes at runtime
Checked exception → compile-time error
Unhandled exception → JVM prints stack trace
```

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**If an exception is not handled, it propagates up the call stack, and if no method handles it, the JVM terminates the program and prints the stack trace.**

## ArrayList vs LinkedList (Java)

Both belong to the **Java Collections Framework** and implement the `List` interface, but they use **different internal data structures**.

---

## 1. ArrayList (Dynamic Array)

Internally uses a **resizable array**.

Example:

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();

        list.add("Java");
        list.add("Spring");
        list.add("React");

        System.out.println(list.get(1));

    }
}
```

Internal structure:

```
Index →   0      1       2
         -------------------
Array → | Java | Spring | React |
```

Access is **very fast using index**.

---

## 2. LinkedList (Doubly Linked List)

Internally uses **nodes connected with pointers**.

Example:

```java
import java.util.*;

public class Demo {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        List<String> list = new LinkedList<>();

        list.add("Java");
        list.add("Spring");
        list.add("React");

        System.out.println(list.get(1));

    }
}
```

Internal structure:

```
Java ↔ Spring ↔ React
```

Each node contains:

```
[prev | data | next]
```

---

## Performance Comparison

### ArrayList Access

```java
list.get(5000);
```

Time complexity:

```
O(1)
```

---

### LinkedList Access

```java
list.get(5000);
```

Time complexity:

```
O(n)
```

Because traversal is required.

---

## Insert Operation

### ArrayList Insert

```java
list.add(1, "NodeJS");
```

Requires **shifting elements**.

```
Time → O(n)
```

---

### LinkedList Insert

```java
list.addFirst("NodeJS");
```

Just updates pointers.

```
Time → O(1)
```

---

## Key Differences

| Feature | ArrayList | LinkedList |
|---|---|---|
| Data structure | Dynamic array | Doubly linked list |
| Random access | Fast O(1) | Slow O(n) |
| Insert/delete | Slow | Fast |
| Memory usage | Less | More |
| Traversal | Faster | Slower |

---

## Example Showing Performance Idea

```java
List<Integer> arrayList = new ArrayList<>();
List<Integer> linkedList = new LinkedList<>();

arrayList.add(10);
linkedList.add(10);

arrayList.get(0);
linkedList.get(0);
```

---

## When to Use

Use **ArrayList** when:

```
Frequent reads
Random access needed
```

Use **LinkedList** when:

```
Frequent insertions/deletions
Queue/Deque operations
```

---

## One-line Interview Answer

**ArrayList uses a dynamic array and provides fast random access, while LinkedList uses a doubly linked list and provides faster insertions and deletions.**

100 Industry-Level Design Patterns Interview Questions

**Design Patterns** and **Architecture Patterns** both help structure software, but they operate at **different levels of abstraction**.

---

**1. Scope**

| Aspect | Design Patterns | Architecture Patterns |
|---|---|---|
| Level | Low-level design | High-level system structure |
| Focus | Classes & objects | Entire application/system |
| Problem | Code design problems | System architecture problems |

---

**2. Example**

**Design Pattern (Factory Pattern)**

Solves **object creation problem**.

```java
interface Shape {
    void draw();
}

class Circle implements Shape {
    public void draw() {
        System.out.println("Circle");
    }
}

class Square implements Shape {
    public void draw() {
        System.out.println("Square");
    }
}

class ShapeFactory {

    public static Shape create(String type) {

        if(type.equals("circle"))
            return new Circle();

        if(type.equals("square"))
            return new Square();

        throw new RuntimeException("Invalid shape");
    }
}
```

Usage

```java
Shape shape = ShapeFactory.create("circle");
shape.draw();
```

This solves **object creation inside code**.

---

**Architecture Pattern Example (Microservices)**

Defines **how the whole system is structured**.

Example structure

```
API Gateway
     |
---------------------
|        |          |
User   Order     Payment
Service Service   Service
     |
Database per service
```

Each service may internally use **design patterns** like:

- Factory  
- Strategy  
- Singleton  
- Observer  

---

**3. Level of Abstraction**

| Level | Pattern Type |
|---|---|
| System design | Architecture Pattern |
| Module design | Design Pattern |
| Class design | Design Pattern |

Example

```
System → Microservices Architecture
Service → Layered Architecture
Code → Strategy / Factory Pattern
```

---

**4. Common Examples**

**Architecture Patterns**

- Microservices
- Monolithic Architecture
- Layered Architecture
- Event-Driven Architecture
- Serverless Architecture
- Hexagonal Architecture
- CQRS
- Event Sourcing

---

**Design Patterns (GoF)**

- Singleton
- Factory
- Builder
- Adapter
- Decorator
- Strategy
- Observer
- Command
- Template Method

---

**5. Relationship**

Architecture patterns **use design patterns internally**.

Example: **Spring Boot Microservice**

```
Architecture Pattern
    Microservices

Inside Service
    Layered Architecture

Inside Code
    Repository Pattern
    Factory Pattern
    Strategy Pattern
```

Example code inside service

```java
@Service
public class PaymentService {

    private final PaymentStrategy strategy;

    public PaymentService(PaymentStrategy strategy) {
        this.strategy = strategy;
    }

    public void process(int amount) {
        strategy.pay(amount);
    }
}
```

---

**Short Interview Answer**

> Architecture patterns define the high-level structure of a system, while design patterns provide reusable solutions for specific problems at the class or object level within that system.

---

**1. Design Principle**

High-level **guidelines / rules** hote hain jo code ko **maintainable, flexible, reusable** banate hain.

Example (Single Responsibility Principle)

```java id="g1c9q3"

    public void calculateTotal() {
        // business logic
    }
}

class InvoicePrinter {

    public void printInvoice() {
        // printing logic
    }
}
```

Idea: **one class → one responsibility**

---

**2. Design Pattern**

Specific **proven solution / template** hota hai jo frequently occurring problem solve karta hai.

Examples

```java id="t3e4hv"
            new Singleton();

    private Singleton(){}

    public static Singleton getInstance(){
        return INSTANCE;
    }
}
```

**Key Differences**

| Feature | Design Principle | Design Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Guideline | Reusable solution |
| Level | High level | Implementation level |
| Purpose | Improve design quality | Solve recurring problem |
| Nature | Conceptual rule | Concrete template |

```text id="w20gl2"
Design principles are high-level guidelines for writing good software design, while design patterns are proven reusable solutions to common design problems.
```

Java **entity["software","Map","Java Collections Framework interface"]** ke multiple implementations hote hain. Interview aur real projects me sabse common implementations:

- **entity["software","HashMap","Java Collections Framework class"]**
- **entity["software","LinkedHashMap","Java Collections Framework class"]**
- **entity["software","TreeMap","Java Collections Framework class"]**
- **entity["software","ConcurrentHashMap","Java concurrent collection class"]**
- **entity["software","Hashtable","Java legacy synchronized map"]**
- **entity["software","WeakHashMap","Java weak reference map"]**
- **entity["software","IdentityHashMap","Java reference-equality map"]**
- **entity["software","EnumMap","Java map optimized for enum keys"]**

Below developer-style quick notes + code.

---

**1. HashMap**

Features  
- O(1) average operations  
- Allows `1 null key`  
- Not thread safe  
- Java 8 → bucket can become **Red-Black Tree**

```java
Map<Integer,String> map = new HashMap<>();

map.put(1,"A");
map.put(2,"B");
map.put(null,"C");

System.out.println(map.get(1));
```

Internal structure

```text
Array -> Bucket -> LinkedList -> RedBlackTree (if size > 8)
```

---

**2. LinkedHashMap**

Features  
- Maintains **insertion order**  
- Used in **LRU cache**

```java
Map<Integer,String> map = new LinkedHashMap<>();

map.put(3,"C");
map.put(1,"A");
map.put(2,"B");

System.out.println(map);
```

Output

```text
{3=C, 1=A, 2=B}
```

LRU example

```java
class LRUCache<K,V> extends LinkedHashMap<K,V>{

    private int capacity;

    LRUCache(int capacity){
        super(capacity,0.75f,true);
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }

    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K,V> eldest){
        return size() > capacity;
    }
}
```

---

**3. TreeMap**

Features  
- Sorted Map  
- Uses **Red-Black Tree**  
- O(log n) operations  
- No null key

```java
Map<Integer,String> map = new TreeMap<>();

map.put(30,"C");
map.put(10,"A");
map.put(20,"B");

System.out.println(map);
```

Output

```text
{10=A, 20=B, 30=C}
```

Custom comparator

```java
Map<Integer,String> map =
        new TreeMap<>((a,b) -> b-a);
```

---

**4. ConcurrentHashMap**

Features  
- Thread safe  
- High concurrency  
- No null keys/values  
- Uses **CAS + bucket level locking**

```java
ConcurrentHashMap<Integer,String> map =
        new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

map.put(1,"A");
map.put(2,"B");
```

Atomic operation

```java
map.computeIfAbsent(10, k -> "value");
```

---

**5. Hashtable**

Features  
- Legacy class  
- Fully synchronized  
- Slower

```java
Hashtable<Integer,String> map = new Hashtable<>();

map.put(1,"A");
map.put(2,"B");
```

---

**6. WeakHashMap**

Feature  
- Entry removed when **key garbage collected**

```java
WeakHashMap<Object,String> map =
        new WeakHashMap<>();

Object key = new Object();

map.put(key,"data");

key = null;
System.gc();
```

Used in **caches / memory-sensitive maps**

---

**7. IdentityHashMap**

Feature  
- Uses **reference equality (==)** instead of `equals()`

```java
IdentityHashMap<String,String> map =
        new IdentityHashMap<>();

String a = new String("A");
String b = new String("A");

map.put(a,"first");
map.put(b,"second");

System.out.println(map.size());
```

Output

```text
2
```

---

**8. EnumMap**

Feature  
- Highly optimized for **Enum keys**

```java
enum Status { OPEN, CLOSED }

EnumMap<Status,String> map =
        new EnumMap<>(Status.class);

map.put(Status.OPEN,"active");
```

Internally uses **array**.

---

**Interview Summary Table**

| Map | Order | Null | Thread Safe | DS |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| HashMap | No | 1 key | No | HashTable + Tree |
| LinkedHashMap | Insertion | 1 key | No | Hash + LinkedList |
| TreeMap | Sorted | No | No | RedBlackTree |
| ConcurrentHashMap | No | No | Yes | Segmented/CAS |
| Hashtable | No | No | Yes | HashTable |
| WeakHashMap | No | Yes | No | Weak refs |
| IdentityHashMap | No | Yes | No | Reference compare |
| EnumMap | Enum order | No | No | Array |

---

- **HashMap internal working (Java 8)**  
- **put() implementation step-by-step**  
- **how collision → treeification works**

with **actual JDK-style code**.

parts: What is difference between design pattern and design principle?

Below is how **entity["java_class","CompletableFuture","Java async computation framework"]** works internally with **entity["java_class","ForkJoinPool","Java work-stealing thread pool"]** and how the async pipeline executes.

---

**1. Default Execution (ForkJoinPool.commonPool)**

If you don’t pass an executor:

```java id="p6a7m1"
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName());
    return 10;
});
```

Runs on:

```text id="2b3xg0"
ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-*
```

---

**2. Internal Structure (simplified)**

```java id="4r1b2k"
class CompletableFuture<T> {

    volatile Object result;     // result OR exception
    volatile Completion stack;  // linked callbacks
}
```

Each stage is a **Completion node**:

```java id="o9z2y1"
abstract class Completion {
    Completion next;
    abstract void tryFire();
}
```

---

**3. Async Pipeline Flow**

```java id="x9c3k8"
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 10)
    .thenApply(x -> x * 2)
    .thenApply(x -> x + 5)
    .thenAccept(System.out::println);
```

Flow:

```text id="l1q7v9"
Task1 (supplyAsync)
   ↓
Completion Node (thenApply)
   ↓
Completion Node (thenApply)
   ↓
Completion Node (thenAccept)
```

Internally stored as a **linked stack of actions**

---

**4. Execution Step-by-Step**

```text id="m4u8c2"
1. supplyAsync submitted to ForkJoinPool
2. Worker thread executes Task1
3. Result stored in "result"
4. All dependent Completion nodes triggered
5. Each node executes (same or different thread)
```

---

**5. Completion Trigger Mechanism**

Core logic:

```java id="z2v7h3"
final boolean complete(Object value) {
    result = value;
    postComplete();
    return true;
}
```

Then:

```java id="n5p1q6"
void postComplete() {
    Completion c;
    while ((c = stack) != null) {
        c.tryFire();
    }
}
```

👉 This is where **pipeline execution happens**

---

**6. Worker Execution (ForkJoinPool)**

```text id="k3m6t1"
Worker Thread
    |
    v
Execute Task
    |
    v
Steal work from other threads (work-stealing)
    |
    v
Execute Completion tasks
```

Work-stealing:

```text id="b7h2s4"
Thread A idle → steals task from Thread B queue
```

---

**7. Sync vs Async methods**

```java id="d1f8g3"
// SAME thread (may block pipeline)
.thenApply(x -> x * 2)

// DIFFERENT thread (async)
.thenApplyAsync(x -> x * 2)
```

Async version:

```java id="e6k2n9"
.thenApplyAsync(x -> x * 2, customExecutor)
```

---

**8. Combining Futures internally**

```java id="c9j4t8"
f1.thenCombine(f2, (a,b) -> a + b);
```

Internally:

```text id="v5r8p2"
Wait for f1 + f2 completion
       ↓
Trigger combined Completion node
```

---

**9. Exception Flow**

```java id="h2u9l5"
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
    throw new RuntimeException();
}).exceptionally(ex -> 0);
```

Internally:

```text id="q1w6e3"
result = AltResult (exception wrapper)
↓
exceptionally() Completion triggered
```

---

**10. Custom Executor (important in real systems)**

```java id="y4p7s2"
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 10, pool)
    .thenApplyAsync(x -> x * 2, pool);
```

---

**11. Full Internal Flow (Interview Diagram)**

```text id="u8c3k9"
submit task
   ↓
ForkJoinPool.commonPool
   ↓
worker thread executes task
   ↓
result stored (success/exception)
   ↓
trigger Completion stack
   ↓
execute dependent stages
   ↓
final result consumed
```

---

**🔥 Senior Interview One-liner**

```text id="t6p1z8"
CompletableFuture uses ForkJoinPool for async execution and maintains a stack of Completion nodes that are triggered upon task completion, forming a non-blocking execution pipeline.
```

---

If you want next level (very important for senior roles), I can show:

- **ForkJoinPool internal (work-stealing queues deep dive)**
- **CompletableFuture performance tuning (CPU vs IO tasks)**
- **Common production mistakes (thread starvation, blocking calls)**

Difference samajhne ke liye 2 method references dekho:

- **Instance Method (Specific Object)** → `object::method`
- **Instance Method (Class Type)** → `ClassName::method`

---

## 1. Instance Method (Specific Object)

👉 Ek **specific object** pe method call hota hai

```java id="j3k9a1"
class Demo {
    void print(String s){
        System.out.println("Hello " + s);
    }
}

Demo d = new Demo();

// method reference
Consumer<String> c = d::print;

c.accept("Prem");
```

Equivalent lambda:

```java id="f8m2q7"
Consumer<String> c = s -> d.print(s);
```

✔ Fixed object  
✔ Argument → method parameter

---

## 2. Instance Method (Class Type)

👉 Object **runtime pe aata hai** (first argument)

```java id="p7n4t2"
List<String> list = List.of("a","bb","ccc");

// method reference
list.forEach(System.out::println);
```

Better example:

```java id="z6w1r8"
BiFunction<String, String, Integer> f = String::compareTo;

int result = f.apply("a", "b");
```

Equivalent lambda:

```java id="y4x9k3"
BiFunction<String, String, Integer> f =
    (s1, s2) -> s1.compareTo(s2);
```

✔ Object comes from first parameter  
✔ Method called on that object

---

## 3. Core Difference

| Feature | Specific Object | Class Type |
|---|---|---|
| Syntax | `obj::method` | `Class::method` |
| Object | Fixed | Passed at runtime |
| Lambda mapping | `x -> obj.m(x)` | `(x,y) -> x.m(y)` |
| Flexibility | Less | More |

---

## 4. Quick Visual

```text id="k9x2w7"
Specific Object:
    d::print
    → s -> d.print(s)

Class Type:
    String::compareTo
    → (s1,s2) -> s1.compareTo(s2)
```

---

## 5. Interview One-liner

```text id="t5q8m1"
In object method reference (obj::method), the instance is fixed,
while in class-type method reference (Class::method), the instance is passed as the first argument at runtime.
```

---

If you want, I can also cover **all 4 types of method references with tricky interview questions** (very common in Java 8 interviews).

```java
}
```

---

**1. Binary Tree**

**entity["data_structure","Binary Tree","Tree where each node has at most two children"]**

Rule  
→ Har node ke max **2 children** (left, right) ho sakte hain  
→ **No ordering rule**

Example

```text id="fd1zqk"
        10
       /  \
      30   5
     / \
    20  2
```

✔ Valid Binary Tree  
❌ Not BST (rules break ho rahe hain)

---

**2. Binary Search Tree (BST)**

**entity["data_structure","Binary Search Tree","Ordered binary tree with left < root < right rule"]**

Rule

```text id="3lq9rf"
Left subtree < Root
Right subtree > Root
```

Example

```text id="g9p6ks"
        10
       /  \
      5    20
     / \
    2   8
```

✔ Valid BST

---

**3. Code Example (BST insert)**

```java id="6g8t2n"
class Node {
    int val;
    Node left, right;

    Node(int val) {
        this.val = val;
    }
}

class BST {

    Node insert(Node root, int val) {

        if(root == null) return new Node(val);

        if(val < root.val)
            root.left = insert(root.left, val);
        else
            root.right = insert(root.right, val);

        return root;
    }
}
```

---

**4. Key Differences**

| Feature | Binary Tree | BST |
|---|---|---|
| Ordering | ❌ No order | ✅ Sorted |
| Search | O(n) | O(log n) (avg) |
| Structure | Any shape | Ordered structure |
| Use case | General trees | Searching, sorting |

---

**5. Important property (BST)**

```text id="0i6y4h"
Inorder traversal → always sorted
```

---

**6. Interview one-liner**

```text id="x2m5pz"
A Binary Tree is a general tree with at most two children per node, 
while a BST is a special Binary Tree where left subtree values are smaller and right subtree values are greater than the root.
```

**Minimal real configuration**

```java
import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class PoolExample {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        ThreadPoolExecutor executor =
            new ThreadPoolExecutor(
                2,                  // core threads
                5,                  // max threads
                60,                 // keepAlive
                TimeUnit.SECONDS,
                new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(10)
            );

        for(int i=0;i<20;i++){
            int task = i;

            executor.execute(() -> {
                System.out.println(
                    Thread.currentThread().getName()
                    + " executing task " + task

            });
        }

        executor.shutdown();
    }
}
```
